en: To delimit what is at stake without inflating the argument, the concept of digital citizenship is mobilized as a parameter, and not as a primer<1><2>398</2></1>. Ribble and Bailey <3>(2007, p. 11)</3> maintain that digital citizenship should not be treated as a rigid set of rules, but as a conceptual lens for understanding the challenges faced by users of technology. Instead of fixing ideas as if they were definitive, the authors defend a guiding approach, aimed at offering criteria and modes of action that help the subject navigate a digital environment that is in constant change. Their formulation makes it possible to treat digital citizenship as an operational grid of what can be governed in the connected environment, without turning the discussion into user blame.

The nine dimensions proposed by Ribble and Bailey <1>(2007, p. 10)</1> function as a minimal map of what makes up participation in the digital realm when enjoyment depends on stable insertion in the ecosystem. They are: digital access (<2>digital access</2>), digital commerce (<3>digital commerce</3>), digital communication (<4>digital communication</4>), digital literacy (<5>digital literacy</5>), digital etiquette (<6>digital etiquette</6>), digital law (<7>digital law</7>), digital rights and responsibilities (<8>digital </8> <9>rights and responsibilities</9>), digital health and wellness (<10>digital health and wellness</10>) and digital <11>p. 381</11> security (<12>digital security</12>). In environments governed by <13>Lex Plataformae</13>, the dimensions cease to appear as competences of the subject and come to be affected by internal rules, architecture, curation and <14>enforcement</14>, becoming governed variables of enjoyment.

Access and literacy, in this framing, are neither a generic inclusion agenda nor a user education program. They are procedural preconditions of contestability within the ecosystem. When enjoyment depends on permanence and recognition, the relevant access is effective access to the functions that make it possible to understand the environment's regime of government, including internal rules, instruments of contestation, decision trails and practical consequences of sanctions or reclassifications. Along the same axis, literacy delimits how far the environment makes it possible to recognize what is happening, why it is happening and how to react, above all when criteria of visibility and of <1>enforcement</1> operate in an opaque or variable way. Without this floor, the informational asymmetry typical of consumption becomes an asymmetry of position. The rule change, the downgrading of reach or the suspension do not even become a verifiable and disputable object within the system itself.

When classifications, visibility criteria and eligibility standards operate without sufficient functional transparency, enjoyment turns into an administered result more than a contestable result. Cohen <1>(2019, p. 43)</1> describes this condition in stating that the operational secrecy typical of the platform environment prevents buyers of these services from easily monitoring the quality of what they have acquired and makes it harder, more broadly, for users to identify whether the company engages in undisclosed forms of preferential placement. The legal-institutional effect is not to impute fault to the supposedly uninformed user, but to recognize that contestability is compressed by design. Vulnerability ceases to be an individual deficit and comes to take the form of administered dependence.

Participating requires executable conditions of speech and conduct. Communication and etiquette function as governable dimensions, because they are mediated by infrastructure and by private rule that distributes reach, organizes attention and applies sanctions through moderation, filters, ranking and metrics. On platforms, communication is not mere exchange between individuals. It is a practice mediated by infrastructure and by private rule that distributes reach, organizes attention and ranks relevance through interface design, moderation, filters, ranking and engagement metrics. What appears as “speech” is speech under technical and normative conditions that operate at the same time as a legitimate form of participation and as an instrument of sanction. Etiquette, in the same sense, is not a manual of good manners. It is the <1>p. 382</1> set of standards that the environment can convert into operational requirements of permanence and visibility, implemented by routines of detection, containment and penalization.

Ribble and Bailey capture the sociotechnical core of this dimension in noting that contemporary forms of mediated communication have created a new social structure that governs who interacts, in what way and at what moment <1>Bailey</1><2>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 19)</2>. The normative correlate appears when they define digital etiquette as the standards of conduct expected by other users of digital technologies<3><4>399</4></3> <5>Bailey</5><6>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 10)</6>. Read within this framework, communication and etiquette cease to be merely diffuse cultural traits and come to operate as governable dimensions of participation, because they structure expectations, define limits of tolerance and delimit the legitimate form of presence in the environment. In these ecosystems, the platform converts patterns of interaction and conduct into technically executable parameters of ordering and sanction, both through explicit rules and through mechanisms of moderation, ranking and restriction of reach. The impact falls directly on the enjoyment position of the consumer-citizen, which comes to depend on signals of conformity, reputation and acceptability produced and applied within the infrastructure itself, with effects on access, visibility, permanence and opportunities for participation.

Under the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>, the “law” does not operate as an external backdrop. It manifests itself as an internal rule that typifies conduct, defines infractions and executes consequences in the ecosystem's infrastructure. There is a structural mismatch. The platform demands conformity as a condition of participation and permanence, but concentrates the power to formulate the normative content, interpret its application and impose sanctions with little reasoning and little openness to contestation. On this reading, the consumer-law lens needs to reach a minimum rationality of <2>enforcement</2> and effective avenues of contestation, or else responsibility will function as a technique of subjection.

Ribble and Bailey's own framing helps keep the focus away from a catalog of crimes and close to the social grammar of acceptability. The authors indicate that respecting laws related to digital technology is only one aspect of digital citizenship, without exhausting it <1>Bailey</1><2>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 131)</2>. The relevant core, for the reading mobilized here, lies in understanding the social reasons for adhering to these rules, critically assessing what is acceptable and considering how actions affect others in society <3>Bailey</3><4>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 131)</4>.

<1>p. 383</1> In platform ecosystems, this framework fits because internal standards of conduct, moderation and sanction cease to be a contingent detail of use and come to operate as a condition of permanence under <2>enforcement</2>. Participation becomes a position conditioned by normative expectations that are translated into operational criteria, applied at scale and with effects that reach access, visibility and continuity of enjoyment. Thus, the debate shifts from the isolated unlawful act to the regime of acceptability that the infrastructure itself institutes, in which the platform defines the threshold of the tolerable, administers deviation and turns adherence to patterns of interaction into a requirement of eligibility.

In the same model, rights and responsibilities describe institutional belonging, and not abstract values. Ribble and Bailey treat digital citizenship as a condition of full membership, in which each user must have rights equitably ensured, while at the same time assuming responsibilities and agreeing to live according to parameters that are mutually agreed upon by the participants <1>Bailey</1><2>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 29)</2>. These limits may take the form of legal rules, regulations or acceptable use policies, and the legitimacy of the arrangement depends, ideally, on the cooperative construction of a framework of appropriate use, at the risk of rules being imposed from the outside in <3>Bailey</3><4>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 29)</4>.

When these parameters are produced, interpreted and executed by private governance, the legally sensitive point is not to demand “good conduct” from the user. It is to delimit what can count as a legitimate parameter and which minimum guarantees make this demand compatible with the institutional asymmetry of the environment.

Digital commerce, finally, is not merely the instant of the transaction. It functions as entry into and maintenance of an enjoyment position in an administered ecosystem, in which the value of the IOC depends on access, visibility, communicability, reputation and continuity. Buying, subscribing to, activating or linking a service of this kind is not equivalent to acquiring an isolated good, but to adhering to a private order that defines conditions of use, eligibility and permanence and can reconfigure these conditions by rule, <1>design</1> and <2>enforcement</2>. For this reason, the typical risk captured by the lens of the CDC is not exhausted in price, quantity, quality or defect in the classic sense. The structural point is the unilateral reconfiguration of the mode of enjoyment and of the criteria that sustain the acquired position, including relevant changes of rules, access standards, visibility parameters, forms of ranking and sanction routines. In IOCs, the transaction buys governed participation, and the degradation of this participation may amount, in practice, to the loss of the enjoyed object itself.

Ribble and Bailey's formulation makes it possible to frame this dimension as mediated economic belonging, without any moralism and without reducing the discussion to individual virtues. <1>p. 384</1> In stating that anyone who works, plays or buys items online is part not only of a digital community, but also of an economic community <2>Bailey</2><3>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 17)</3>, the authors shift the gaze to the fact that presence in these environments involves, simultaneously, social interaction and insertion in circuits of value. For this framing, the point is to consolidate that the economic dimension is part of the very conditions of participation in the ecosystem, because enjoyment does not occur in a normative vacuum, but in a space of conditioned access, in which the platform defines the practical terms of permanence and circulation.

In IOCs, this dimension tends to materialize as maintenance of an enjoyment position in an administered environment, since internal rules, architecture and <1>enforcement</1> reconfigure not only the experience, but also the scope of what it is possible to do, see and continue doing. Economic belonging, in this sense, is not merely the making of a purchase, but dependence on an internal regime that administers eligibility, distributes visibility and decides the continuity of the bond. The consequence is that the legal discussion is not limited to the price or the content delivered, since it involves the daily governance of access and permanence, in which metrics, reputation, conduct and conformity with internal standards can directly influence the possibility of continuing to enjoy what was acquired.

The dimensions of health and wellness and of security complete the picture because, in platform ecosystems, they do not describe merely “risks of use”, but structural conditions of permanence in an environment governed by metrics of performance, comparability and exposure. Enjoyment depends on continuous and recognizable presence, and this presence is stabilized by technical incentives of repetition, by regimes of visibility and by mechanisms of sanction that modulate attention, conduct and self-restraint. On this reading, wellness is an institutional effect of an architecture that produces intensity of engagement, pressure to update and functional risk of loss of access or reputational degradation. Likewise, security should not be read as mere individual prudence, but as self-protection in an environment in which informational asymmetry is the rule and in which the platform itself defines the standard of what counts as safe conduct, acceptable risk and incident response. In legal terms, this shifts the center of the problem to the configuration of risk by the supplier, through the design of flows, internal policies, authentication standards and routines of verification and contestation. The consequence is that integrity and identity cease to operate as strictly personal attributes and come to be administered as practical requirements of credibility and permanence.

The definitions proposed by Ribble and Bailey <1>(2007)</1> make it possible to sustain this framing with low noise, because they delimit “health and wellness” as the set of elements of physical and psychological <2>p. 385</2> well-being linked to the use of digital technologies <3>Bailey</3><4>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 31)</4>. In the same movement, the authors treat “security” as a practice of self-protection that is not exhausted in the individual. Thus, protecting equipment and data is also a duty with community effects, and digital security includes preventing harm to oneself and to others in the face of potentially harmful external influences, going beyond mere care for the hardware <5>Bailey</5><6>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 33–34)</6>. Read under the <7>Lex Plataformae</7>, these dimensions cease to be advice to the user and come to operate as points at which the ecosystem administers risk, permanence and credibility.

Once the <1>Lex Plataformae</1> has been described as practical normativity in operation, the subject of immaterial consumption cannot be reduced to an acquirer. Enjoyment depends on conditions of access, permanence, visibility, communication and reputation administered by internal rules and by <2>enforcement</2>. The appropriate figure is that of the consumer-citizen, consumer because they acquire and expect enjoyment and “citizen” in the analytical sense that they participate under private normative conditions that organize belonging and continuity, with collective effects on recognition and symbolic circulation.

In this framework, Ribble and Bailey provide a minimal grid for naming what is at stake in this participation without moralizing individual competences. When these dimensions are governed by private architecture, curation and sanction, they become institutional variables of the product itself and, therefore, a matter of structural vulnerability. Hence the need for reinforced duties of the supplier compatible with the power exercised, aimed at making controllable rule changes, reconfigurations of access and <1>enforcement</1> measures that degrade the acquired enjoyment position.

The passage from consumption to governed participation shifts the problem to a plane in which vulnerability ceases to be a mere informational deficit and comes to take on institutional density, because enjoyment depends on conditions whose meaning and application take place within the ecosystem. It is this kind of mutation, when technical changes and market arrangements alter the mechanics of harm and render usual categories of protection insufficient, that authorizes legal reconstruction<1><2>400</2></1>.

When technical mediation converts interaction into screening and permanence into performance, coercion tends to operate as administered freedom. Han describes this <1>p. 386</1> mechanism in maintaining that the digital society of control makes intensive use of freedom, precisely because it depends on voluntary self-exposure and self-transparency to function<2><3>401</3></2> <4>Han</4><5>(Han, 2017, p. [13-14])</5>. In this framework, exclusion and degradation of reach cease to be accidents and come to figure as a functional risk of a regime of governed participation, in which permanence depends on continuous alignment with operational and reputational standards.

In view of this, the next step requires neither rhetorically broadening the critique nor nationalizing the platform. The necessary movement is to convert the diagnosis into operational normative criteria that bear precisely on the points at which private power reconfigures access, permanence, communication and sanction. For this reason, auditable and controllable parameters will be formulated below, with reinforced duties compatible with the asymmetry, such as qualified transparency, minimum stability of enjoyment conditions, restoration in the face of degrading changes or sanctions, open auditability and functional equivalence, articulated with the axes of integrity and identity.

<1>Digital Citizenship in Schools</1>, by Mike Ribble and Gerald Bailey (2007), organizes the debate into a finite set of dimensions and has become established as a recurrent reference in the human and social sciences. Its usefulness, here, lies not in prescribing individual virtues, but in offering a stable taxonomy for naming practical conditions of participation in the connected environment that, in platform ecosystems, can be administered by internal rules and by infrastructure of classification and sanction. Incorporating this grid gives contour to what is understood as participation in the digital realm and prevents the problem from being reduced to contractual etiquette or shifted to individual responsibility. The full procedure of the integrative review carried out to select the theoretical framework regarding the concept of digital citizenship presented is available in the article entitled “Buscando um conceito operacional de cidadania digital: uma revisão integrativa da literatura estrangeira no pós-COVID-19”, published by the author, co-authored with professors Vanessa Corsetti Gonçalves Teixeira and Luciana Lopes Canavez, in INTER, Revista de Direito Internacional e Direitos Humanos of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro <2>Andrade</2><3>(Andrade; Teixeira; Canavez, 2022)</3>. <4>↩</4>

When students see adults using technologies inappropriately, they assume that this is how they should act.” <1>Bailey</1><2>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 24)</2>. <3>↩</3>

For Han, the turn of digital control lies less in surveillance “from outside” and more in the active adherence of the participants themselves, who communicate, expose themselves and feed the system as a condition of belonging: “Initially, the internet was celebrated as a medium of boundless liberty. […] Today, unbounded freedom and communication are switching over into total control and surveillance. More and more, social media resemble digital panoptica keeping watch over the social realm and exploiting it mercilessly. […] Jeremy Bentham’s panopticon isolated inmates from each other for disciplinary purposes and prevented them from interacting. In contrast, the occupants of today’s digital panopticon actively communicate with each other and willingly expose themselves. That is, they collaborate in the digital panopticon’s operations. […] Accordingly, data is not surrendered under duress so much as offered out of an inner need. That is why the digital panopticon proves so efficient.” <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, p. If the platform simultaneously governs meaning, access, reputation and sanction, the starting point is not “information” understood as content communicated to the consumer, but the regime of intelligibility of the ecosystem itself. What is in dispute, in the consumption of IOCs, is the possibility of enjoyment existing as a stable and recognizable position over time. This position depends on a grammar of signs that makes the experience legible and comparable, on access paths that make certain practices possible and others impracticable, on circuits of visibility that convert recognition into a condition of value and on devices of <1>enforcement</1> that reconfigure the continuity of enjoyment through restrictions, downgrades and exclusions. When these four dimensions are administered by the same decision center, vulnerability ceases to be merely an asymmetry regarding contractual data and becomes <2>p. 387</2> structural dependence on the way the environment produces value, distributes belonging and decides permanence.

Semiotic vulnerability arises because, in this kind of supply, the object is not “worth” something only for the content delivered, but for the socially operable meaning that the ecosystem manages to stabilize around the user's position. The environment decides which signals will be sufficient to produce prestige, which metrics will define performance, which categories will organize comparability and which marks of trajectory will be preserved as recognized memory. Thus, the consumer faces not only the lack of access to information about price, risk or limitations, but the practical impossibility of mastering the vocabulary and the criteria that attribute economic meaning to what was acquired. The deficit is semiotic because it falls on the production of legibility and commensurability of the object itself; it is institutional because this production is concentrated, mutable and scarcely verifiable for those who bear its effects.

This vulnerability becomes more acute when the governance of meaning is coupled with the governance of access. The platform not only describes what the user “can” do, but implements the range of the possible through architecture: permissions, frictions, interface patterns, verification requirements, calendars, availability windows and interaction sequences. The consequence is that the consumer's formal autonomy turns into administered autonomy. Deviant conduct need not be prohibited; it suffices that it be made expensive, slow, invisible or technically impracticable. Access, here, is a normative-operational category: it defines what exists as a real possibility of enjoyment and, therefore, is part of the very content of the supply.

Next, the platform governs reputation and visibility as variables of value. The user's position in the ecosystem is not merely “being inside”, but being found, being considered eligible, being comparable and remaining recognizable under signals that circulate publicly. <1>Rankings</1>, performance metrics, signals of prestige, recommendations and forms of highlighting operate as the economic language of the environment: they convert attention into opportunity and convert recognition into permanence. In this layer, vulnerability is not an individual weakness, but rather the fact that the positional value of the IOC depends on internal criteria of classification and exposure that can be unilaterally recalibrated, without sufficient publicity of the grounds and without proportional means of contestation. Reputation, therefore, is not a side effect of consumption, but rather a governed component of the enjoyed object.

<1>p. 388</1> The integration of these dimensions is completed by <2>enforcement</2>. Sanctions, downgrades and restrictions do not function as an exceptional response to a fully intelligible infraction, since they operate as gradual instruments of everyday governance. A decisive part of <3>enforcement</3> occurs through visibility and eligibility: remaining “inside”, but less findable, less rankable, less recommended and less recognized may amount to a relevant loss of the object in its functional and symbolic value. The sanction, in this arrangement, need not present itself as clear punishment to produce functional dispossession. It suffices to reorganize the conditions of access, reputation and continuity of enjoyment so as to degrade the acquired position, maintaining the formal bond while altering the practical core of what was enjoyable.

In view of this design, legal control cannot be reduced to a checklist of abusive clauses, because the injury may occur without textual alteration and without evident contractual breach. The effective shaping of the IOC is produced by continuous operations of the ecosystem, and the central risk is the unilateral reconfiguration of enjoyment by opaque operational criteria. Clauses are relevant, but do not exhaust the phenomenon, since the decisive power lies in the capacity to define and execute, through infrastructure, the parameters of legibility, comparability, eligibility and sanction. The focus of control needs to fall on the practical rationality of the regime: which criteria exist, how they are applied, how they can be verified and which avenues of contestation are effectively usable.

Hence the demand for operational and institutional criteria. Qualified transparency does not mean “more information” in the abstract, but intelligibility of the criteria that structure enjoyment: classification standards, recommendation parameters, minimum reasons for downgrades and restrictions, explanation of the type of conduct or signal that triggered the measure, and communication capable of enabling an informed response. Effective contestability requires that the challenge not be a mere ritual, but an avenue with deadlines, stages, access to minimum elements of the grounds and a real possibility of review. Verifiable reasoning is not justificatory rhetoric; it is the minimum form of transforming decisions into examinable objects, making it possible to control coherence, proportionality and non-discrimination.

Open auditability comes in as a requirement of external verifiability and of control over “how” the decision was produced. It is not a matter of demanding full exposure of trade secrets, but of making decisive categories auditable, including <1>logs</1> and records of measures applied, decision trails, general eligibility criteria, error statistics, correction mechanisms, and guarantees that the system does not operate by irrecoverable arbitrariness. Auditability is “open” because it needs to be compatible with scrutiny beyond the unilateral <2>p. 389</2> account of the platform itself, lest contestation remain blind and the conflict remain trapped in the result.

Functional value equivalence operates as a yardstick to capture the point at which the platform preserves the formal appearance of the supply, but degrades its real utility. If the IOC is an enjoyment position in a governed environment, reducing functionalities, limiting relevant access, imposing asymmetric frictions, downgrading eligibility or reorganizing visibility may substantially alter what the consumer is able to do, even without “removing” the nominal object. Functional equivalence makes it possible to frame these mutations as a possible loss of the object in its economic core, requiring restoration when the enjoyment delivered ceases to correspond, in operational terms, to the legitimately expected level.

Integrity and identity complete the path because, in the IOC regime, they are not mere subjective adornments, but rather structural dimensions of value when the ecosystem governs belonging and continuity through reputation, social memory and recognized trajectory. Integrity, here, concerns the minimally consistent preservation of the conditions of enjoyment and participation that allow the consumer to remain legible and operative, without arbitrary reconfigurations that destroy the practical unity of the experience. Identity, in turn, designates the recognizable continuity of a position built through records, repertoire, signals of prestige and bonds, whose destruction through downgrades or exclusions may produce functional dispossession and collapse of commensurability. When these elements are administered by the infrastructure, they become legally relevant as part of the protected object: the platform administers not only access to utilities, but the possibility of continuity of a socially recognized position that was economically built within the ecosystem itself.

Thus, the transition from semiotic vulnerability to operational criteria is not rhetoric of protective expansion. It is a reconstruction of the point of incidence of control: from the textual promise to the effective regime of value production, in which meaning, access, reputation and sanction are integrated as a mechanism of private governance. If the power that reconfigures enjoyment is exercised through architecture and through information, the legally adequate response requires parameters that also operate at this level: intelligibility of criteria, verifiability, contestability, auditability, functional equivalence and mechanisms of restoration proportional to the density of the dominion exercised.

So far, enjoyment has appeared as a position sustained by signs, visibility and equivalences that exist only while the environment keeps them operative. Under this condition, acquisition depends on an ecosystem that supplies intelligibility, commensurability and the possibility of sanction, while at the same time defining, in practice, access, permanence and hierarchies. For this reason, the description of the IOC, when it seeks to support legal control, cannot remain confined to the vocabulary of price or to the psychological repertoire of preference. The core is institutional, because the platform administers the conditions of enjoyment and, in so doing, stabilizes value as a recognizable position, even when the relevant experience is reconfigured over time.

The aim is neither to build a general constitutional theory of platforms nor to transpose categories of public power automatically onto private relations, but to delimit a minimal analytical framework in which the platform is read as an instance of practical governance, with enough economic and informational power to organize access, permanence and participation at scale.

When the offer materializes as ecosystem-dependent enjoyment and value is anchored in hierarchies, criteria and sanctions produced by the environment itself, private power ceases to be merely a competitive fact and comes to act as a structural component of vulnerability, so that consumer protection must engage with limits and duties <1>p. 331</1> proportional to the intensity of the control exercised, without dissolving the problem into abstractions and without reducing the platform to the classic figure of the supplier indifferent to how the very market it administers operates.

The investigation opened with the hypothesis that, in the digital environment, the platform tends to take over, by technical and contractual means, functions that were previously distributed across society, replacing public criteria of circulation and recognition with private rules of access, visibility and permanence. The formula according to which the platform “occupies the place of the collectivity without authorization” is treated as a descriptive problem to be stabilized in verifiable institutional terms, lest it remain an intuition without legal consequence.

This hypothesis must be stabilized in controllable institutional language. What matters is to identify which operations make up this occupation, what effects it produces on the enjoyment position and what asymmetries it creates between the consumer and the administrator of the ecosystem, so as to allow conduct, duties and restoration to be assessed without relying on impressionistic readings of the conflict. To this end, it must be recognized that, in the IOC regime, the platform does not merely intermediate a bilateral relationship between supplier and acquirer. It organizes, simultaneously, the normative content of the environment and the mechanisms for enforcing it.

First, it defines and updates internal rules that structure access and permanence, establishing permissions, incentives and punishments through moderation, functional restrictions or exclusions. Second, it administers visibility and reputation as economically relevant dimensions, through metrics, rankings, signals of prestige and instruments of public comparison that produce hierarchies and modulate the experience. Third, it exercises continuous curation of what appears, what disappears and what returns, controlling the horizon of expectation and reorganizing the temporality of consumption. Finally, it applies sanctions and restrictions whose effects go beyond the loss of a one-off utility, degrading symbolic position, interrupting continuity of enjoyment and reconfiguring the economic meaning of the IOC, in a register close to functional and identity dispossession.

Describing these powers requires no assumption of subjective intent, because what is at stake is a mode of operation in which control is exercised through architecture and through information. In digital environments, the relevant normativity does not manifest itself only as an explicit command, but as a configuration of choices, rhythms, frictions and incentives that makes certain conduct more likely and other conduct more costly, while defining the criteria by which the environment itself will recognize, reward or sanction the user. This governance is carried out through <1>design</1> decisions, moderation parameters, recommendation patterns and <2>p. 332</2> access rules that operate as silent infrastructure, so that coercion need not present itself as outright prohibition in order to produce obedience, predictability and conformity.

As a result, the consumer faces not merely a contract, but an integrated set of devices that guide the experience and stabilize hierarchies while keeping the actual operating criteria opaque, creating a structural asymmetry between those who live in the ecosystem and those who control the variables that define its conditions of legibility, permanence and value.

It is in this strict sense that the expression “without authorization” should be understood, not as a generic political judgment, but as the finding that the platform performs functions of social ordering without holding a public mandate and without submitting, to an equivalent degree, to demands of institutional reciprocity. The relevant absence is not that of formal delegation, but that of minimum guarantees that function as counterweights of legitimacy, such as intelligible disclosure of criteria, the possibility of verification, decisional coherence, accessible reasoning and effective avenues of challenge.

When the environment is governed by mutable rules, selective curation and technical <1>enforcement</1>, the user is subjected to decisions that can alter their enjoyment position and degrade the value of the IOC without the grounds of the act being transparent, without its proportionality being open to examination and without review being practicable on terms commensurate with the economic and identity relevance of what is at stake. Consequently, private power consolidates itself as a power to administer symbolic and economic destinies at scale, while preserving a functional opacity that prevents the consumer from turning the conflict into an object of rational control, shifting the experience of enjoyment into a regime of institutional dependence not recognized as such.

Once this structure is recognized, the consequence for consumer law cannot be framed as a mere rhetorical expansion of protection, but as an adjustment of lens capable of reaching the way the offer actually materializes. If the IOC exists as a governed enjoyment position and value depends on internal criteria of recognition, protection cannot settle for reading the contract as an exhaustive statement of content, because the object is actually shaped by rules, architecture and continuous operations that go beyond the documentary form and can unilaterally alter the continuity of supply.

The question, therefore, is not merely to identify isolated abusive clauses, but to understand that the environment itself functions as a mechanism that produces vulnerability, which makes duties proportional to the power exercised relevant. The task, <1>p. 333</1> then, is to prepare a conceptual basis that allows transparency, stability and restoration to be demanded on terms compatible with the regime of permanence and with the institutional density of the platform, without yet anticipating the dogmatic reconstruction developed later, but establishing that protection must reach the architectural plane on which enjoyment becomes possible and on which risk is actually administered.

To accomplish this task without generalizations, the discussion that follows will draw on references with delimited functions, as instruments of description and conceptual anchoring. With Julie E. Cohen <1>(2012; 2019)</1>, the text delimits the specific form of power that stabilizes when information and architecture become means of practical governance, which makes it possible to treat choices, patterns and infrastructures as normative mechanisms that organize conduct and distribute possibilities. Warren and Brandeis <2>([201-?])</2> serve as a methodological model of legal reconstruction in the face of technical changes that reconfigure exposure and vulnerability, indicating that changes in the material conditions of social life require categories to be reinterpreted without moralizing the phenomenon. Byung-Chul Han <3>(2015; 2017)</3> is used as a lens to describe adherence and self-adjustment through performance, comparison and expectation, characterizing subjection as a structural effect of incentives and of the management of symbolic risk rather than attributing it to individual frailties. Eros Grau <4>(2008)</4> provides the conceptual anchor that avoids both the liberal neutralization of private normativity and its hasty transposition into the category of the State, making it possible to describe it as presupposed law endowed with collective effects and, therefore, requiring control criteria commensurate with its density.

The expected result is to establish a conceptual key according to which the platform, in the IOC regime, operates as a private power with practical normativity, because it administers not only conditions of exchange but conditions of enjoyment and recognition in a governed environment. This key moves the debate away from the simplifying opposition between freedom of contract and state intervention toward a plane on which internal rules, design, curation and <1>enforcement</1> constitute the economic object itself and distribute risks of loss, exclusion and degradation of value.

This prepares the transition to operational criteria that will make it possible to discuss proportional duties, transparency standards and restoration mechanisms without relying on merely formal categories, because the relevant materiality of the IOC will be understood as functional and ecosystemic materiality, and not as mere abstract ownership or one-off performance.

Governance by architecture is taken as the starting point to show how the platform constitutes a normative environment in which choices are configured and in which <1>p. 334</1> informational domination is carried out by administering the variables that make enjoyment legible, comparable and sanctionable. This form of power is not confined to the economic dimension, since the technical reorganization of the conditions of exposure, participation and permanence calls for a pattern of legal reconstruction capable of dealing with new forms of vulnerability at scale, without this implying that the platform becomes a State.

In the same vein, the consumer's subjection is treated as a structural effect of mechanisms of performance, comparison and self-adjustment, when the ecosystem turns recognition into a condition of value and converts the management of symbolic risk into an instrument for shaping conduct, so that identity captivity emerges as an institutional outcome and not as an individual pathology.

The analysis then turns to the framing of private rules and <1>enforcement</1> as practical normativity, showing how the <2>Lex Plataformae</2> operates as the effective law of the environment and administers access, reputation, curation and sanctions with effects of exclusion and functional dispossession. This path closes with the figure of the consumer-citizen<3><4>370</4></3> subjected to this private normativity, making it visible that consumer protection, when dealing with the IOC, must engage with the institutional impact of platform governance and prepare the way for structuring concepts that turn the description of power into an object controllable by criteria of transparency, stability and restoration.

The expression “consumer-citizen” is used in a strictly analytical and functional sense. It designates the holder of an IOC, an immaterial product whose utility is realized as permanence in an ecosystem rather than as an isolated delivery. The “citizen” component does not refer to classic political-constitutional status or to nationality, but describes the practical conditions of participation, belonging and continuity within an environment governed by private rules and technical sanctions (Lex Plataformae). The point is to recognize that, in continuous digital consumption, the subject is subject to a private normative order that administers their visibility, reputation and capacity to act, making the enjoyment of the product inseparable from their position as a governed member of the ecosystem. <1>↩</1>

The techno-media economic order of digital consumption does not operate only as a market structure, infrastructure and continuous extraction of value. It projects itself, with equal force, onto the plane of signs and attention, where value and delivery are no longer perceived as stable attributes of a “good” and come instead to be constituted by administered visibility, reputation, metrics and belonging. In platform ecosystems, enjoyment is not reduced to using a feature. It involves participating in a governed symbolic grammar, in which prestige, rarity, recognition and experience are part of the content delivered as perceived, and in which the promise is fulfilled through codes of reading and through equivalences built within the environment.

To make this regime knowable, semiotics is treated here as a material dimension of the legal problem, not as interpretive ornament. The consumption promise is stabilized by signs, interfaces and regimes of representation that define what “counts” as delivery and which equivalences are socially recognized as value. In this vein, the contribution of Umberto Eco<1><2>280</2></1> makes it possible to understand how codes and conventions make the performance legible and organize the consumer's expectations, whereas Guy Debord<3><4>281</4></3> brings out the centrality of the spectacle and of the circulation of images in shaping desire and adherence. Jean Baudrillard<5><6>282</6></5> completes the axis by showing how, in attention economies, simulacrum and hyperreality shift the center of the commodity to its symbolic efficacy, so that consumption presents itself as access to experiences and positions, and not merely as the acquisition of discrete utilities.

<1>p. 262</1> This semiotic plane, however, does not operate in a vacuum. It is governed. The platform appears as an instance of private administration that organizes enjoyment through architecture, rules and <2>enforcement</2>, defining access, permanence and visibility. This includes both explicit decisions, such as policies and sanctions, and decisions embedded in <3>design</3>, in curation and in the metrics that select what will be seen, rewarded and reproduced. Governance, in this sense, is not an “accessory” to consumption, but an operational condition of the performance itself. The contribution of Julie E. Cohen<4><5>283</5></4> is drawn on to describe the platform as a form of organizing power that produces dependencies, structures conduct and naturalizes patterns of participation through technical and institutional means not exhausted by the contract.

The asymmetry that matters on this plane is not exhausted by a deficit of available information. It takes shape as an inequality of codes and language regimes that condition what the consumer can perceive, compare and contest within the environment. Luis Alberto Warat<1><2>284</2></1> and Maurizio Gnerre<3><4>285</4></3> are drawn on for this precise function, developing and fixing the perspective according to which vulnerability may arise from the gap between operational languages and languages of enjoyment, between vocabularies of promise and vocabularies of control, and between system metrics and expectations of experience. Semiotic vulnerability thus remains a structural category, tied to intelligibility and agency, and not an individual pathology or a mere absence of “enlightenment”.

The legal problem deepens when this governance comes to have total effects on the consumer's presence and reputation within the ecosystem. The prudential reference of Samuel <1>p. 263</1> D. Warren II<2><3>286</3></2> and Louis D. Brandeis<4><5>287</5></4> serves as a methodological model for recalibrating categories in the face of technical mutations that reconfigure the scope of rights and expectations, preventing the legal response from remaining trapped in material analogies that no longer reach the real experience of enjoyment. Next, Byung-Chul Han<6><7>288</7></6> is drawn on to name psychopolitical dimensions of adherence and induced self-government, in which the bond is sustained by the pressure of performance, comparison and continuous validation. Eros Roberto Grau<8><9>289</9></8> helps to recognize that normativity can operate as an effective order imposed by an organization endowed with power, making it possible to characterize as practical governance what presents itself as a “condition of use” or “internal rule” but produces structural effects on ways of life and social positions in the digital environment.

In this context, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer is not merely informational. It is structural, semiotic and institutional. It is structural because it stems from concentrated control over infrastructure, rules and channels of visibility. It is semiotic because it bears on the production of the very codes of value, reputation and delivery equivalence. It is institutional because it is stabilized by private procedures of adjudication, sanction and unilateral modulation, often opaque and difficult to contest. The relevant vulnerability is not exhausted by a “lack of information”. It involves an asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in an environment in which the consumer depends, in order to enjoy and to exist socially, on grammars, metrics and access regimes administered by the supplier.

The aim here is to make explicit how the capture of meaning and governed participation become constitutive components of continuous immaterial consumption, making legally visible losses and frictions that do not appear as classic nonperformance, but as degradation of enjoyment, a lowering of perceived value and the erosion of belonging through <1>p. 264</1> technical and governance decisions. Semiotic vulnerability is thereby stabilized as a structural asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in platform ecosystems, and the mechanisms by which enjoyment comes to depend on regimes of visibility, metrics and private sanction are outlined, to a degree sufficient to allow later legal qualification without relying on a demonstrative empirical narrative.

A graduate in Philosophy of the <1>Università di Torino</1>, Umberto Eco was an Italian semiotician, philosopher, medievalist and cultural critic, known both for his academic contribution to semiotics and the theory of interpretation and for his public profile as a writer. In 1975, he took up the chair of Semiotics at the <2>Università di Bologna</2>, where he also held academic leadership positions in communication and performing arts studies. <3>↩</3>

A graduate of the undergraduate program in Philosophy at the <1>Université de Paris</1> (Sorbonne), Guy Debord was a Marxist theorist, filmmaker and one of the leading figures of the Situationist International, an artistic and political movement active from the 1950s to the 1970s. Although his career was not academic in the strict sense, he is recognized for his role in the critique of consumer society, of symbolic alienation and of the use of the image as an instrument of social domination. His work offers a radical analysis of the logic of the spectacle as a form of organization of life under late capitalism, and of particular relevance to this research is the book <2>La Société du Spectacle </2> (“A Sociedade do Espetáculo”, in the Brazilian edition), originally published in 1967. <3>↩</3>

Holder of a doctorate in Sociology from the <1>Université Paris X</1> (Nanterre), Jean Baudrillard was a French philosopher, sociologist and cultural theorist with broad influence in communication studies, postmodern critique and the philosophy of language. He is known for his critique of the culture of simulation and of the dissolution of reality into regimes of signs, especially in advanced consumer societies. <2>↩</2>

Cohen is an American legal scholar and a leading reference in law and technology, with prominent work on privacy, surveillance, intellectual property and platform governance. She is a professor at <3>Georgetown University Law Center</3>, where she researches how informational infrastructures and legal arrangements reconfigure institutions and power relations in the contemporary economy. <4>↩</4>
