The development of the structuring categories of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption thus begins with semiotic vulnerability, established as a specific form of vulnerability in platform-governed markets of enjoyment and serving as the <1>p. 396</1> legal translation of the already consolidated diagnosis of continuous consumption, practical normativity and governance by infrastructure. Enjoyment is not merely promised in the abstract, but continuously shaped by an environment that implements rules, orders priorities, modulates visibility and executes sanctions, so that access, permanence, circulation and reputation become part of the very mode of existence of the object. The purpose of the category is to offer a key for description and control capable of representing the decisive inequality in these environments, in which value, belonging and recognition are mediated by signs, by regimes of visibility and by internal mechanisms of commensuration.

The relevant vulnerability does not arise, therefore, from one-off informational asymmetries, but from a structural asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in relation to the arrangement that governs enjoyment. When the environment controls the parameters of appearance, recognition and commensuration that structure value and belonging, and keeps opaque the criteria for distributing consequences, the possibility of planning conduct, anticipating effects and contesting decisions is structurally weakened. The problem then shifts from "knowing more" to "being able to orient oneself and react". That is, enjoyment may remain formally accessible and, even so, degrade through chronic instability and through compression of contestability.

Semiotic vulnerability may be defined, in summary, as the objective condition of the consumer's exposure to a structural inequality of intelligibility and agency in platform-governed ecosystems of enjoyment, in which the production of meaning and the attribution of value depend on codes, metrics and regimes of visibility administered by the environment itself. It is vulnerability because the consumer finds themselves subjected to internal criteria that qualify conduct, rank appearances and shape objective conditions of enjoyment derived from the nexus between the promise of the object, as presented in the offer, and its effective delivery, as executed by the architecture of the service, without having equivalent means to fully understand the operating logic, contest its parameters or influence the distribution of consequences.

By way of illustration, the <1>mobile</1> version of the empirical laboratory studied is taken as a reference. If, on the computer, the intermediate currency already shifts the price into the fiefdom and forces the consumer to make conversions to understand how much what was bought costs, in <2>League of Legends: Wild Rift</2> this same logic is reorganized for an environment of compartmentalized attention, notorious for facilitating impulse decisions. In the <3>mobile</3> environment, it is not enough to translate reais into an internal currency. Value itself comes to be distributed across a constellation of economic signs that coexist at the same time, with different functions and <4>p. 397</4> different access, which prevents the consumer from stabilizing a simple cost reference. The game's paid currency fulfills this role of gateway, but it does not close the account, because consumption branches into parallel currencies linked to rewards, performance and events, and each one creates a small circuit of its own within the same service <5>Riot Games +1</5><6>(Riot Games, 2022l; Riot Games, 2025l; Riot Games, 2021d)</6><7><8>410</8></7>.

The consequence, here, is not “complexity” in the neutral sense, as if it were merely a variety of systems. What sets in is a structural inequality of intelligibility. The consumer no longer deals with a price that can be compared and audited in a straight line, and instead deals with multiple internal grammars that require situational reading, because each currency “speaks” a different language. In the classic <1>desktop</1> version, it is still possible to reconstruct, calmly, the equivalence between the expenditure and the item acquired, above all when the store operates with a dominant monetary core. In the <2>mobile</2> environment, however, this core no longer holds. The experience is designed to operate in fragments of time, and value itself is fragmented along with it, as if the platform were telling the consumer that understanding “how much it costs” is a private effort, which needs to be produced within the game, “however possible” and “with whatever attention is left”. This difficulty is not a neutral side effect of the variety of systems, but operates as a deliberate puzzle, transferring to the consumer the burden of deciphering an economy that the environment designed to be costly to read.

This becomes even more evident when one analyzes how consumption is remodeled into strictly temporary microeconomic dynamics. Events set up their own stores, with their own currencies that exist and remain valid under their own individual deadlines. Enjoyment, then, depends not only on the purchase, but also on the ability to keep up with short windows, spend at the right time and accept that certain balances expire. For the consumer playing with partial attention, in intervals, the intelligibility of value comes to depend on a schedule and on a set of internal conversions that are updated as content flows. The urgency need not be shouted, because it is already embedded in the <1>p. 398</1> mode of operation, insofar as <2>tokens</2> are tied to dates and cease to exist after a certain period <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2022n; Riot Games, 2022m)</4><5><6>411</6></5>.

Likewise, the instability of the real cost is not limited to the internal design of the store. It also appears when the platform adjusts economic parameters by region and runs bonuses that reconfigure, window by window, the perceived advantage of buying paid currency. As a result, the consumer faces not merely an intermediated price, but an intermediated price whose “purchasing power” is affected by future decisions and by promotional regimes, so that external equivalence becomes even less able to serve as an anchor of control. What, on PC, was already opacity induced by conversion and by bundles becomes, on <1>mobile</1>, an even more asymmetric condition of use, because consumption occurs under intermittent attention and under an economic regime that multiplies, expires and recalibrates <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2021e)</3><4><5>412</5></4>.

The qualification as semiotic is not anchored in individual deficits of attention, reading or rationality, nor is it to be confused with a psychological description of use. It refers to the structure of the sign system that organizes the experience and that conditions what appears as delivery, as success, as failure and as loss within the ecosystem. Under the theoretical lexicon of Umberto Eco <1>(1991; 2000)</1>, the environment not only communicates information about the object, but structures the field of interpretation in which enjoyment becomes intelligible, so that control of the decisive codes and mediations reconfigures the very possibility of decoding and reaction by the consumer.

<1>p. 399</1> At this point, before going further in describing how semiotic vulnerability operates today in platform-governed ecosystems, a basic methodological point should be fixed. The inequality of intelligibility that structures enjoyment and its relevant losses is not born with the digital. It is an earlier mechanism, linked to the unequal distribution of decoding competence and to the monopoly of codes that condition access to understanding, to participation and to power. It is in this sense that Warat<2><3>413</3></2> and Gnerre<4><5>414</5></4> are drawn on to establish, in controllable language, that decoding asymmetry is a mode of power asymmetry and that specialized languages can operate as barriers of exclusion.

Warat makes this core explicit when treating the semiology of power as an analysis of how signification can function as an instrument of social control, a normalizing and disciplinary strategy and a consensus-producing formula, capable of fabricating effects of verisimilitude over the material conditions of social life <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>. In this key, the asymmetry of intelligibility is not a psychological defect of the consumer, but a discursive technology of government. Objectively, the author maintains that the legitimacy of power depends on discursive work and can be obtained through suitable manipulation of words, which shifts the appearance of publicity and formal validity to the plane of its strategic production <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</4>.

This operation is reinforced when one recognizes that the stability of meaning is sustained by prior ideological coincidence, so that the belief in normative univocity and in the unalterability of signifiers does not stem from naivety, but functions as a condition of social efficacy of the ideal of the rational legal norm <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 68)</2>. For this reason, obedience can be produced without explicit command, since the social idiom tends to constitute an ordered subjectivity, making it possible to dispense with physical violence and converting it into <3>p. 400</3> signifying violence or imaginary violence, through which social cohesion is maintained by means of the creation of phantasmatic significations<4><5>415</5></4> <6>Warat</6><7>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</7>

Gnerre describes language as a mechanism for blocking access to power, stating that “language constitutes the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power” <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 22)</2>, and defines the social function of closed codes in noting that “special languages” “exclude from communication the people of the linguistic community external to the group that uses the special language”<3><4>416</4></3> <5>Gnerre</5><6>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 23)</6>. In platform-governed ecosystems of enjoyment, this mechanism tends to be radicalized when the grammar of signs, metrics and visibility, which is part of the performance itself, comes to be administered and executed as infrastructure, converting inequality of decoding into practical inequality of agency and contestation in the IOC regime.

In the empirical laboratory under study, this mechanism can be observed without any theoretical sophistication, merely by paying attention to the use of a single word. Upon entering the <1>League of Legends</1> store, the command offered to the consumer user displays the word “buy”. This is not a neutral verb. Both common sense and even the Brazilian Civil Code itself<2><3>417</3></2> use the verb “buy” in the sense of acquiring something that becomes “yours”, meaning that one expects minimum stability, permanence and <4>p. 401</4> some form of control over what was acquired. Even when one knows that it is a digital item, the idiom of purchase and sale automatically triggers this typical expectation and functions as an interpretive shortcut.

The grammar of acquisition does not end with the verb "buy". It extends into the organization of the inventory as a "collection", an expression that also carries its own patrimonial and semiotic density. Collecting does not mean merely gathering items. It means ordering a collection, recognizing rarity, comparing value, preserving history, completing series, displaying belonging and building a relationship of continuity between subject and object. The collector, in the ordinary social use of the word, is someone who holds qualified dominion over what they collect, even though this dominion may take different legal forms depending on the type of good involved. When the platform presents digital content as part of a collection, it mobilizes this cultural expectation of permanence and turns isolated items into a patrimonial biography, even though, on the contractual plane, the same content is described as an access license tied to the account. For this reason, any account block, removal of an item, substantial alteration of functionality or architectural devaluation of the collection does not affect merely a detachable digital unit. It affects the intelligibility of the collection itself as a bundle of continued enjoyment, whose value depends on internal recognition, minimum stability and preservation of the relationship between the consumer, their items and the ecosystem that gives them meaning.

Alongside this surface grammar, however, there is the technical grammar of the contract. The Terms of Service describe the same items as “Virtual Content” offered under an access license tied to the account <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. As a consequence, what the interface presents as a “purchase” is requalified by the contractual instrument as conditioned and institutionally administered access. The point is not to claim that the consumer “did not read” or “did not understand”, but to recognize that the ecosystem itself organizes the decision through a sign that frames the relationship as a typical contract, while reserving, on the legal plane, a regime that does not coincide with the ordinary meaning of the verb “buy”.

It is in this friction, simple and verifiable, that semiotic vulnerability becomes intelligible. The relevant asymmetry is not merely lack of information, since information may exist and, even so, not operate as practical guidance when the language of the interface governs the experience and stabilizes expectations in real time. The platform controls the signifiers that shape the perception of what is being acquired and, at the same time, controls the institutional criteria that define what the consumer actually comes to have.

The result is an objective inequality of decoding and agency, because the consumer decides under the grammar of “buying”, but enjoyment takes place under the grammar of the <1>p. 402</1> “revocable license” attached to the account. This does not justify claiming that the use of the word “buy” is, in itself and in isolation, unlawful. The issue is that, without a core that respects the minimum stability of the good, even the superficial parallel becomes false and therefore leads to the breach of the legitimate expectation of enjoyment, and only then is unlawfulness established. The aim is not to prevent the use of typical expressions, but to guarantee that the expectation is minimally met, by assigning responsibility for the auditability of alterations and requiring the preservation of equivalent functionality whenever a legitimate alteration occurs.

With these premises established, it becomes possible to advance to the properly contemporary description of semiotic vulnerability. The contribution of Warat and Gnerre consists in demonstrating that language, code and decoding competence have been, since before the digital, factors of unequal distribution of power and of exclusion from participation. In platform-governed regimes of enjoyment, however, this mechanism ceases to operate merely as a discursive barrier or filter of access to formal arenas and comes to bear on the very delivery of the object, since enjoyment takes place through technical mediations that administer visibility, recognition and attribution of value. Under this framework, semiotic vulnerability is justified as a category for qualifying the IOC regime, preparing the analysis, in the keys of Eco, Debord, Baudrillard and Vanderburg, of the way in which signs, commensuration and regimes of appearance structure enjoyment and its relevant losses.

In environments of continuous consumption, visibility does not operate as a mere aesthetic attribute of the experience, but as a structuring mechanism for ordering and allocating value. The circulation of the object, the perception of its relevance and the way the consumer is positioned in the ecosystem come to depend on criteria of appearance, prominence and accessibility that are defined by the environment and executed through technical mediations. What becomes available for enjoyment, what becomes recognizable as achievement and what becomes identifiable as failure cease to be self-evident and become outcomes administered by internal rules and by hierarchies of exposure.

In this key, Guy Debord's contribution makes it possible to describe how the regime of appearance reorganizes experience and guides conduct through the management of what is seen, what is valued and what becomes socially relevant. When visibility is converted into an infrastructure of recognition and commensuration, the environment not only distributes attention, but shapes the objective conditions of enjoyment and normalizes losses and restrictions as part of the ordinary operation of the service. Semiotic vulnerability then manifests itself as the consumer's dependence on a regime of appearance that can expand, reduce or <1>p. 403</1> reorder value and belonging without resorting to explicit commands, merely through continuous modulation of the conditions of circulation and prominence.

The centrality of visibility becomes even more decisive when the value of the object ceases to be exhausted in its functional utility and comes to incorporate, as a relevant economic component, the sign-value associated with distinction, prestige and position. In certain ecosystems, what is acquired is not reduced to access to content or to an isolated functionality, since it includes the possibility of being seen, recognized and validated under the internal rules of circulation. Under these conditions, enjoyment involves a relational and public dimension that is part of the core of the object, so that value depends on the permanence and intelligibility of symbolic marks administered by the environment.

Jean Baudrillard's key makes it possible to understand why relevant losses can occur without total suppression of access or formal interruption of the performance. When sign-value is part of the good, alterations that persistently downgrade the consumer's position, erase their visibility, degrade their reputation or restrict their circulation can produce a loss equivalent to the loss of the object itself, even if the “content” remains technically available. Semiotic vulnerability, at this point, reveals that the decisive asymmetry does not consist merely in knowing more or less about the product, but in controlling the criteria of valuation and recognition that determine whether enjoyment preserves, in substantial terms, the economic and social meaning that justified the acquisition.

Semiotic vulnerability is organized in two complementary faces, whose distinction is relevant to avoid diluting the concept into a generic formula. The structural face stems from the very technical-organizational arrangement that governs enjoyment, since the environment produces dependence on meaning and recognition by establishing the codes, metrics and regimes of visibility through which the experience becomes intelligible and socially valued. The consumer's position is asymmetric because the parameters that define what appears, what circulates, what counts as success and what presents itself as failure are defined by internal instances and executed continuously, conditioning their agency.

The strategic face emerges when the administration of this symbolic grammar becomes an instrument of exploitation. In this case, the same set of mediations that organizes enjoyment can be used to induce conduct, distribute costs and normalize losses by means of selective opacities, asymmetric frictions, reorderings of visibility and gradual adjustments that corrode the enjoyment bundle without producing, immediately, a perceptible total rupture. The distinction between these faces makes it possible to recognize that semiotic vulnerability is not limited to an inevitable scenario of technical mediation, but also provides language to identify <1>p. 404</1> when the structure of the ecosystem is mobilized in a way oriented toward exploitative purposes, without this identification depending on express contractual commands or ostensibly abusive textual promises.

Before going further in describing semiotic vulnerability in its properly contemporary form, two essential limits should be raised. The first concerns the intensification of vulnerability through choice architecture and through the action of controlling intermediaries, capable of shaping conduct and reactions through technical mediations. The second concerns performative transparency, whereby information exists but does not turn into practical intelligibility when excess and incomparability function as operational noise within the environment.

In this context, the intensification of vulnerability through architecture is not limited to a diffuse environmental effect, since it can be described in a dogmatic key as a mode of managing behavior and the very form of performance. In continuous and platformized digital contracts, control over choice paths, frictions, rhythms of contracting and conditions of permanence shifts the asymmetry to the plane of execution, in which the consumer's decision is shaped by technical mediations and by intermediaries that do not act as simple neutral channels.

Along these lines, Claudia Lima Marques<1><2>418</2></1> notes that “now vulnerability and the new harms also come from the design and the action of the intermediating third party”, adding <3>p. 405</3> that this digital intermediary is the “access guardian (gatekeeper)”, increasingly dominant in the contractual “time” and “mode” <4>Marques</4><5>(Marques, 2024, [p. 3])</5>. The consequence, for the category of semiotic vulnerability, is that the asymmetry of intelligibility and agency can be produced and exploited by the interaction architecture itself, making the design of options and of avenues of reaction legally relevant as part of the fact that intensifies vulnerability in the IOC regime.

This point becomes sharper when interface patterns are described as a sanctionable commercial practice, since abusiveness ceases to depend on an isolated textual statement and comes to include the way choices are presented and induced. In this sense, the authors note that “several of these provisions are related to dark patterns, which allows us to conclude that under the Brazilian legal framework it is possible to sanction several cases of deceptive design” <1>Bergstein</1><2>(Marques; Mendes; Bergstein, 2023, [p. 4])</2>. The relevance, for the IOC regime, lies in recognizing that vulnerability can be intensified by choice architecture and by presentation techniques that reorganize the perception of risk and hinder reaction, even if the supplier's formal discourse remains neutral or ostensibly “transparent”.

The problem worsens when transparency is simulated through excess, dispersion or heterogeneity of information and conditions, so that the multiplication of options and descriptions comes to function as an obstacle to comparability and, therefore, to the practical intelligibility of what is being supplied. In a different context, but with a directly transposable mechanism, Wada<1><2>419</2></1> observes that “it was very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks, since there were countless products included and, in most cases, they did not correspond to the competing bank's offer”, a circumstance that led to the issuance of a resolution to pre-establish services and “facilitate consumers' comparison” <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 168-169)</4>. The relevant point is that information may exist and, even so, remain innocuous as an instrument of control when the environment organizes the offer so as to prevent substantive comparison and assessment, converting formal compliance into operational noise. Under this logic, semiotic vulnerability includes the consumer's exposure to <5>p. 406</5> communicational structures that appear open, but produce opacity by making the formation of comparative judgment and the identification of relevant degradations unfeasible.

Semiotic vulnerability intensifies because technical mediation does not operate merely as a neutral channel of access, but as a form of routinization of expectations and dependencies. In Vanderburg's theoretical perspective, this process can be described as the everyday sedimentation of forms of mediation that naturalize patterns of conduct and evaluation, converting certain frictions, downgrades and restrictions into expected components of the experience. The consequence is that relevant degradations can be internalized as a "normal cost" of the service, which weakens the capacity to identify the harm and shifts contestation to a terrain in which the decisive criteria remain opaque or unavailable. Semiotic vulnerability, at this point, is not merely the difficulty of obtaining information, but exposure to a regime in which the very measure of what counts as loss is produced by the environment that distributes losses.

The description of this vulnerability requires attention to the technical ecology in which enjoyment occurs, so that the concept is not reduced to an abstract reading of the sign disconnected from the forms of mediation that produce and stabilize it. Under Postman <1>(2006)</1> and Ellul <2>(1968)</2>, technique imposes rationalities, rhythms and criteria of pertinence that reorder social experience and make certain consequences predictable without their being presented as explicit normative decisions.

Such mediations reveal that design and organization are not elements external to the object, but choices that structure possibilities of action and distribute costs in the regime of enjoyment, defining frictions, incentives, forms of circulation and parameters of recognition that make certain losses more likely than others. In Feenberg's key, these choices can be treated as socially situated and, therefore, susceptible to legal description when they produce persistent asymmetries of intelligibility and contestation.

Recognizing this dimension does not imply converting every design decision into unlawfulness, but authorizes the analysis of design as a form of infrastructural power capable of guiding conduct and normalizing harm by means of technical and organizational patterns. With this, it becomes possible to prepare a language of attribution that reaches purposes inscribed in the architecture of the service, especially when the mediation structure is mobilized to produce dependence, selective opacity and relevant degradations without the need for express contractual commands.

Even when there are formal clarifications about rules of use or about abstract possibilities of alteration, the decisive asymmetry remains when the environment retains for itself the <1>p. 407</1> administration of the codes of valuation, the regimes of visibility and the internal criteria that qualify conduct and distribute consequences. Informing, in this picture, describes the risk in generic terms, but does not give back to the consumer equivalent means of understanding, verifying and contesting the decisions that reconfigure their position.

For this reason, legal protection needs to reach the practical normativity produced by infrastructure, under which relevant degradation can result from persistent modulations of visibility, reputational downgrades, selective functional restrictions and internal sanction mechanisms that do not present themselves as textual nonperformance, but operate as erosion of the enjoyment bundle. Semiotic vulnerability, by shifting the focus to the governance of the sign and of mediation, prepares the demand for criteria that make such effects verifiable and attributable, without reducing control to an episodic assessment of formal consent.

Official support describes the paid currency of Wild Rift and states that Wild Cores is “an in-game currency, bought with real money”, in addition to noting that it is “the equivalent of RP in Wild Rift” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022l)</2>. The document indicates that acquisition can take place “directly in the app”, linking the purchase to the payment settings of the device's store <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2022l)</4> and facilitating the purchase procedure for the user. The support page then highlights: “Poro Coins are a new monetary unit exclusive to Wild Rift!” <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2025l)</6>. The mobile ecosystem stands out for adding currencies that are not directly confused with the paid currency, reinforcing the multiplication of internal economic signs. In this sense, the Ranked Store page notes that “Ranked Coins stay with you from one season to the next, allowing you to save up to buy the best items in the Ranked Store” <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, 2021d)</8>, which shows that the game operates simultaneously with purchase currencies and multiple functional currencies tied to regimes of participation and performance, expanding in scale and depth the process of internal monetary fragmentation. <9>↩</9>

In an official event communication for <1>Wild Rift</1>, support notes: “As per the information above, the Emblem Store will remain open for one week after the end of the event.” <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2022n)</3>. The passage is relevant for recording the way temporality operates, in very short windows, as a condition of consumption, and not merely as a kind of informative calendar. In another event, support notes: “Even after you stop earning Emblems on the 11th, you will still have a whole week to spend them. Afterwards, they will disappear forever [...]." <4>Riot Games</4><5>(Riot Games, 2022m)</5>. Here, it is shown that urgency does not depend on an external emotional appeal, because expiration is designed as a rule of the token system itself. Thus, by adopting as a procedure the creation of multiple currencies that are not confused with one another and have multiple durations within the ecosystem, including expiring entirely when their scheduled period ends, the platform stands out for further aggravating the user's difficulty in understanding the real value of what they are able to acquire, giving rise to and mobilizing, above all, the fear of missing out in its users. <6>↩</6>

In this sense, by way of illustration, an official <1>Wild Rift</1> news item records price adjustments by region and mentions, for Brazil, “+15% average price increase” <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2021e)</3>. In the same piece, <4>Riot</4> describes a period of “double bonus currency” associated with purchases of virtual currency, that is, a temporary reconfiguration of the perceived advantage of acquiring paid currency, meant to offset the temporary negative impact that an adjustment of this magnitude tends to have on the consumer base <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2021e)</6>. It is important not to forget, in this context, that <7>Riot</7>'s contractual terms allow alteration of the “purchasing power of the Game Currency”, including by increasing the number of coins needed to acquire virtual products, and expressly deny any value “in money or otherwise” to virtual content associated with the account <8>Riot Games</8><9>(Riot Games, 2024e)</9>.The contract also acknowledges future adjustment of prices and billing methods, with an impact on the purchasing power of the currency <10>Riot Games</10><11>(Riot Games, 2024e)</11>. It should also be stressed that the same Terms of Service apply both to the <14>desktop</14> version of <12>League </12> <13>of Legends </13>and to all the company's other games, including <15>League of Legends: Wild Rift</15>. <16>↩</16>

Entitled <1>O Direito e sua Linguagem</1>, the work of Luis Alberto Warat <2>(1984)</2> directly introduces the problem of language in Law, setting aside the idea that legal discourse would operate as a neutral instrument of naming. Based on semiotic references and a critical perspective on the functioning of signs, Warat maintains that legal language performs directive, persuasive and ideological functions, organizing meanings and producing effects of authority. It is the mechanism according to which asymmetries of decoding and mastery of the code are capable of operating as spheres of power asymmetry, which provides a methodological basis for understanding why the inequality of intelligibility is not a “digital” phenomenon and can be radicalized by distinct technical mediations. <3>↩</3>

In the work <1>Linguagem, escrita e poder</1>, Maurizio Gnerre <2>(1991)</2> investigates the relations between verbal language, the technology of writing and social hierarchies, rejecting the reading of language as a simple vehicle of information and insisting on its role as a marker of position and instrument of authority. In discussing the “cultivated” norm, normative grammar and the historical legitimation of standardized varieties, the author shows how “special languages” and regimes of correctness function as mechanisms of exclusion and discrimination, associated with political and ideological processes. Gnerre's contribution to this discussion lies in offering a conceptual framework for describing how technical codes and institutionalized languages can operate as competence barriers, creating structural asymmetries of access to meaning that predate the digital and that, in platform-governed ecosystems, tend to turn into practical infrastructures of mediation, visibility and validation. <3>↩</3>

For Warat, the most efficient obedience does not depend on direct command or on continuous physical coercion. It stabilizes when power organizes social meaning through “devices of signification”, disciplines bodies by linking desire and power and converts force into a violence that operates on the plane of the imaginary: “[The] power produced consolidates its reproductive conditions through ‘devices of signification’, which organize society and its institutions, and ensure the presence of power when force is lacking. It is through its ‘devices of signification’ that power disciplines bodies, causing the members of a society to link their desires to power. […] The ‘social idiom’ ends up constituting an ‘ordered subjectivity’ […] that makes it possible to gradually dispense with physical violence, transformed into ‘signifying violence’, into ‘imaginary violence’. […] Society keeps itself cohesive by resorting to the creation of phantasmatic significations […]” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Gnerre shows that the “blocking” is not a moral metaphor. It is a very concrete social technique, which operates both in the production and in the comprehension of messages and is reproduced through “special” phraseologies and lexicons that filter belonging and capacity to act. “As we have already noted, the problem is, on the one hand, one of comprehension of messages and contents and, on the other hand, one of production of messages. Starting from the most elementary level of relations with power, language constitutes the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power. […] The central function of all special languages is social: they have a real communicative value but exclude from communication the people of the linguistic community external to the group that uses the special language and, on the other hand, they have the function of reaffirming the identity of the members of the small group that has access to the special language.” <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 22-23)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In the 2002 Civil Code, purchase and sale appears as a typical and nominate contract, governed in Book I (Law of Obligations), Title VI, specifically in Articles 481 et seq. Its classic structure is the exchange of a thing for a price, with reciprocal obligations in which the seller undertakes to transfer ownership of the thing and the buyer to pay the price in money, preserving the idea of acquisition and of minimum stability of the good in the acquirer's patrimony, except in specific cases provided by law. “Art. 481. By the contract of purchase and sale, one of the contracting parties undertakes to transfer ownership of a certain thing, and the other, to pay it a certain price in money.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]a)</2>. On the conceptual plane, this framing is relevant because the verb “buy”, in ordinary social use, refers directly to this contractual type and to its core of transfer of classic, physical and material property in things, which tends to trigger typical expectations of acquisition that are distinct from regimes of revocable access license. <3>↩</3>

For discussion of the theme, the article <1>Vulnerabilidade na era digital: um estudo sobre os fatores de </1> <2>vulnerabilidade da pessoa natural nas plataformas</2>, by Claudia Lima Marques and Guilherme Mucelin (2022), stands out for its investigation, based on the dogmatics of Consumer Law, of how traditional factors of vulnerability are projected into the digital environment, identifying vulnerabilities specifically linked to the platformization of consumption. The text is mobilized as a dogmatic basis to maintain that vulnerability intensifies when the architecture of the environment and the design of interactions are capable of managing choices and conduct, shifting the focus from mere informational deficit to the way infrastructure organizes agency, intelligibility and risk in continuous digital services. Further, in <3>A evolução do contrato de prestação de </3> <4>serviço digital e a necessidade de proteção do consumidor: para lá do comércio eletrônico</4>, Claudia Lima Marques <5>(2024)</5> maintains that the digital consumer market has gone beyond the paradigm of electronic commerce and has come to operate through continuous and platformized arrangements, in which the consumer's relationship with the object takes place through technical mediations and controlling intermediaries. The article serves as a framing key for the continuous digital contract and its typical asymmetries, contributing to ground the need for categories capable of representing how performance takes place through governance in operation, with effects on expectation, participation, visibility and restoration when enjoyment is degraded. In the article <6>Dark patterns e padrões </6> <7>comerciais escusos</7>, Claudia Lima Marques, Laura Schertel Mendes and Laís Bergstein (2023) describe deceptive practices incorporated into interface <8>design</8> and discuss how such techniques can manipulate consent and choice in the digital consumer market, articulating the legal response through the dialogue of sources. The article contributes by objectively recognizing the possibility of treating design as a legally relevant dimension of commercial practice. Thus, the authors maintain that design would prove capable of structuring asymmetries of agency and normalizing losses through frictions, <9>defaults</9>, acceptance paths and regimes of visibility, reinforcing the reading according to which vulnerability in the IOC is not exhausted in information provided, but involves governance of behavior through architecture, a reading perfectly coherent with the theoretical construction of Julie E. Cohen, studied in the previous chapter. <10>↩</10>

Another relevant contribution to the discussion derives from <1>A proteção do consumidor contra as práticas comerciais </1> <2>abusivas no código de defesa do consumidor: novo ensaio para sistematização e aplicação do direito do </2> <3>consumidor</3>, the doctoral thesis of Ricardo Morishita Wada <4>(2016)</4>, in which the author proposes a systematization of abusive commercial practices in the CDC, with special attention to the structural effects of certain offer and market architectures on comparability and control. Especially relevant is the instrument Wada offers for treating opacity and “transparency” as problems of structure, not as one-off communication failures, making it possible to describe situations in which the appearance of informational compliance coexists with mechanisms that degrade practical intelligibility and hinder control and attribution. <5>↩</5>

The qualification of the immaterial object of consumption within the Consumer Protection Code requires bringing platform-governed enjoyment back into a dogmatic framework that preserves the object as an object, without reducing its existence to a one-off delivery event and without dissolving it into an undifferentiated notion of service that erases what was actually acquired. Anchoring the IOC in the concept of product in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC operates as a starting point because it maintains the intelligibility of supply even when enjoyment depends on technical mediations and on governance in continuous operation. The purpose is to fix operable contours for the category, so that it organizes the reading of the offer, makes it possible to identify relevant losses and prepares criteria of attribution and restoration in continuous consumption, without inaugurating an autonomous microsystem and without depending exclusively on explicit contractual commands or episodic informational duties.

The legal definition of product in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC operates as a scope clause that prevents escape from protective coverage when the object does not present itself in the form of a physical medium. Nunes<1><2>425</2></1> makes explicit that the CDC's choice of “product”, rather than narrower civil law categories, has the function of encompassing material and immaterial goods, noting that the designation applies to economically offered objects that are not tangible, when stating that “the designation ‘product’ is used, for example, in banking activities (loan, fixed-income investment, pledge of securities etc.). Such ‘products’ fit, then, into the definition of immaterial goods” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 97])</4>. This framework shifts the discussion from the medium to the function of the acquired object and to the form of its enjoyment, preserving the possibility of qualifying <5>p. 412</5> relevant losses even when formal access to the content remains available. The same reasoning is reinforced when the author states that “banks sell products”, distinguishing “the immaterial ones commented on before and the material ones such as money” <6>Nunes</6><7>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 102])</7>, dispelling the idea that the immaterial would correspond to a legally ungraspable “non-object”.

Continuity, in turn, is not an element foreign to the CDC, nor does it prevent the dogmatic qualification of supply. Nunes maintains that services can be durable when they present continuity over time by contractual stipulation, observing that durable services are those that have continuity by reason of what was agreed and giving as examples school services, health plans and, in general, every service that the contract establishes as continuous <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 102])</2>.

In continuing bonds, the risk of unilateral reconfigurations and interruptions is part of the very structure of enjoyment as a lasting relationship, which prevents treating utility as something already delivered and definitively beyond discussion whenever formal access persists. This trait appears directly when the author identifies as proper to contracts for continuous services those whose mark is continuity “ad infinitum as long as the consumer fulfills their obligation to pay the price” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508])</2>. Continuity, thus, functions as a property of the supply bond and not as a pretext for dissolving the object into generic activity.

The distinction between product and service, when treated in an operable way, is an instrument of qualification and not a rigid dichotomy. Nunes stresses that there are cases in which the performance is correctly qualified as a service even when there is delivery of something physically identifiable, since the core lies in the supply and in the infrastructure that ensures availability. When dealing with public services, he points out that “it is important to stress this aspect of the service that is accompanied by the product, to avoid doubts regarding the public service, because even if it delivers some product (e.g., water), it continues to be characterized as a service” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 113])</2>, adding that “in reality it is the ‘supply’ that is the service rendered. “The assembly of the entire transmission network, piping, sanitation etc. is done so that the service may be rendered” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 114])</4>.

This key makes it possible to describe situations in which enjoyment depends on continuous infrastructure, but nevertheless involves the acquisition of an identifiable core of utility, preserving the intelligibility of the object and preparing to confront the product-service tension without reductionism.

<1>p. 413</1> The reconstruction of the IOC as a category internal to the CDC requires, in addition to dogmatic support for qualification, a methodological foundation capable of disciplining the translation of the factual regime into operable legal language<2><3>426</3></2>. It is this foundation that prevents the concept from appearing arbitrary, also serving as an obstacle to the alibi of “technical necessity” as a strategy for immunizing institutional design<4><5>427</5></4>.

Mangabeira Unger's critique<1><2>428</2></1> turns against the institutional fatalism that converts the platform's design into fatality and presents it as “technical necessity”<3><4>429</4></3>, that is, as something external to the field of the controllable. On the explanatory plane, Mangabeira Unger confronts both “deep structure” theories, which treat social formations as indivisible totalities governed by laws of development, and certain versions of positivist social science, which describe social life as negotiation of interests within a setting taken as given.

<1>p. 414</1> Against these traditions, the author radicalizes the thesis that society is a human and contingent artifact. He maintains that prevailing institutions and beliefs are provisional settlements produced by past conflicts, and not the realization of necessary imperatives. In doing so, he places institutional design back in the field of the revisable<2><3>430</3></2> and prevents the present from being confused with the only possible horizon of humanity <4>Unger</4><5>(Unger, 2004, p. xx)</5>.

This methodological brake gains special relevance when the platform justifies itself through a language of impersonal coordination<1><2>431</2></1>, presenting hierarchies, frictions and authorization regimes as neutral requirements of operation. Unger makes it possible to render this movement visible by indicating that, in the modern legal imaginary, different social spheres are usually organized by distinct “modes” of containing power, and that the organization of work is frequently associated with the combination of voluntary agreement and the invocation of an “impersonal technical necessity” <3>Unger</3><4>(Unger, 2004, p. 301-302)</4>.

From a critical perspective, this grammar can operate as an unjustified restriction of institutional possibilities, insofar as it shifts controversies about design and domination to the register of the inevitable. In this key, the existence of technical restrictions is not denied, but their functioning as a seal of immunity is refused. If the utility consumed depends on an environment that modulates access, visibility, updating and <1>enforcement</1>, <2>p. 415</2> governance by architecture must remain tractable by criteria of verifiability and attribution.

The effect of inevitability is consolidated when the very structure of the regime is withdrawn from the field of deliberation and comes to appear as the “natural” backdrop of relations, ceasing to be perceived as a revisable arrangement. Unger describes this mechanism when pointing to the effort to depoliticize the basic structure of rights and economic policy and when noting that, once the original conflicts and uncertainties are forgotten, the institutional settlement takes on a misleading appearance of naturalness and necessity<1><2>432</2></1>, although it derives from contingent interests, illusions and tactical results <3>Unger</3><4>(Unger, 2004, p. 178)</4>. This warning prevents the practical normativity exercised by architecture from being treated as an inevitable exteriority and keeps open the field of the controllable, so that architectural decisions that shape enjoyment can be qualified, proven and attributed by minimally verifiable dogmatic criteria.

Next, the central methodological requirement that follows from Reale is that the legal category operate as integration and remain referred to the concrete conditions it organizes. In defining the norm as the “moment of integration of a class of facts according to an order of values”, the author makes explicit that the normative structure only becomes intelligible when referred to the factual and axiological factors that it dialectically integrates <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 96)</2>.

<1>p. 416</1> This key makes it possible to present the IOC as an instrument of qualification that integrates a stabilized social and technical fact, namely sustained enjoyment governed by infrastructure, with normative values recognized in the protective consumer regime, and with a legal language capable of guiding the identification of the object, the recognition of relevant losses and criteria for restoration.

This operation of integration imposes limits against arbitrariness and also against the temptation to convert the concept into technological moralization. Reale maintains that, even if the idea of Natural Law is not adopted, the elaboration of legal norms cannot disregard natural data that impose themselves on everyone's ethical or scientific conscience <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 1994, p. 109)</2>. The same limit appears when he rejects the notion that objective law is made up of empty shells, since normative structures are not mere logical forms without content. For Reale, they are forms that derive from a concrete experience, whose dominant lines are abstracted from social reality to operate as instruments of social discipline, that is, as legal models <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 1994, p. 110)</4>.

This conception of the norm as a model prevents the framing from being voluntarist and requires anchoring in observable elements of the regulated phenomenon itself. The result is a double lock, because the category must capture dominant lines of the concrete experience of sustained enjoyment and infrastructural governance, and must do so through verifiable elements, preventing any ordinary friction from being converted into an unlawful act through intuitive repulsion. At the same time, it must preserve the core of value of the acquired object and make it possible to distinguish ordinary variations of the digital regime from significant degradations of the enjoyment bundle, lest it lose its disciplinary function.

The three-dimensional theory provides direct justification for treating the formulation of the IOC as a response to regularities of social experience and as a regulatory choice conditioned by facts and values, and not as a free exercise of will. Reale maintains that “the elaboration of a given and particular legal norm is not a mere expression of the arbitrariness of power, nor does it result objectively and automatically from the factual-axiological tension operating in a given historical-social conjuncture”, since it is a culminating moment of legal experience, “but power always being conditioned by a complex of facts and values, in light of which the option is made for one of the possible regulatory solutions […].” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 1994, p. 61)</2>.

In complement, the idea of “legal models” is linked to the technical translation of social regularities into operable forms. Reale maintains that the very possibility of legal science presupposes the existence of relations endowed with stability and predictability and, in short, of certain “constants of action”, at least within a certain historical conjuncture, without <1>p. 417</1> which it would make no sense to contemplate rules intended to govern the order of human acts <2>Reale</2><3>(Reale, 1994, p. 106)</3>. In this framework, the model does not function as a descriptive ornament, because the concept of model, in any kind of science, is linked to the idea of logical planning and to the symbolic and anticipated representation of results to be achieved by means of an ordered sequence of measures or prescriptions <4>Reale</4><5>(Reale, 1994, p. 111)</5>. What matters, for this framing, is that this representation does not arise from nothing nor is it legitimized by conceptual elegance, since it depends on identifying dominant lines of social experience and converting them into parameters that guide decisions and allow control.

In this sense, the legal model is a way of making the conflict tractable with criteria, while preserving the link with the facts and values that give meaning to the normative intervention. In environments of governed enjoyment, in which architecture, internal rules and <1>enforcement</1> combine to define conditions of access and permanence, the controversy tends to escape traditional categories if they do not capture what repeats and what is decisive in practice. The IOC, here, operates as a technique for representing the conflict because it organizes, in a single analytical frame, the core of value that the consumer acquires and the infrastructural conditions that sustain the continuity of this enjoyment. It thus makes it possible to describe precisely what is in dispute when unilateral reconfigurations, screenings, eligibility criteria and visibility standards alter the bundle of promised utilities, without reducing the problem to intuitive impressions or to moralizations about technology. By transforming these regularities into controllable elements, the IOC makes the conflict decidable, that is, susceptible to dogmatic qualification and legal response, without breaking the link with the concrete experience that justifies its existence.

The qualification of the IOC as an infrastructure-concept also requires an instrument to explain why dogmatics needs to stabilize expectations and produce criteria of decidability in an environment marked by structural asymmetry of intelligibility and by continuous mutation of the conditions of enjoyment.

Ferraz Jr.<1><2>433</2></1> makes explicit that dogmatics does not eliminate uncertainty, but works on it in a controlled way to make the conflict decidable without breaking the binding to norms, when stating that, with the “controlled term”, one intends to signify that dogmatics “increases uncertainties”, but <3>p. 418</3> does so in a way compatible with “two central requirements of the legal discipline”, which are “the binding to norms, which cannot be ignored, and the pressure to decide conflicts, since a way out must be found for them” <4>Jr.</4><5>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 44])</5>. The IOC, at this point, does not exist to “describe” the digital, but to bring sustained enjoyment, reconfiguration and <6>enforcement </6>back to a vocabulary that allows attribution and restoration without arbitrariness.

The same movement is articulated with the stabilizing function of norms as durable expectations, which resist empirical frustration counterfactually. Ferraz Jr. explains that normative attitudes are expectations whose durability is guaranteed by “non-adaptive generalization”, and concludes that norms manifest expectations “stabilized counterfactually”, since generalization “is independent of the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of the empirically expected action” <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 98])</2>. This formulation preserves the core of promise of the object even when technical execution, curation and sanctions executed by design make enjoyment unstable and subject to unilateral reconfiguration.
